articles.title: Abolish Lock Poisoning
articles.summary:
Rust has a curious feature that I don’t think the language would land today,
if it was not there for a long time: mutex poisoning.  When some Rust code
panics while holding a std::sync::Mutex, the mutex is poisoned.  That means
that any further call to lock() returns a PoisonError.  The motivation for
this feature is that an object might have some internal invariants that need to
be upheld and panicking in the wrong moment might invalidate reasonable at and leave an
object behind in a broken state.
Personally I absolutely hate this feature as it has bitten me so many times and
I cannot once remember it helping me.  The libs team is
discussing making the
non-poisoning locks the default in the next edition but entirely expectedly it
has caused quite a few people to jump to the defence of the feature.
In this post I want to make my personal case why poisoned locks should either
be entirely removed or be made the exception.
Primarily this is because I have yet to come across code in the wild that
handles a poisoned lock correctly.  On the other hand I have come across enough
code that mishandles it and as a result behaves worse than a
parking_lot lock would which does not support
poisoning.
Josh Triplett put it quite
strongly in a hackernews comment: “In the entire history of the standard
library, we have never once seen a single report of anyone attempting to recover
from poison.”
When a panic happens with a lock held, there are two reasonable reactions: shut
the process down, or carry on and ignore the flag.  With panic = "abort" you
get the former and poisoning never comes up.  From all the evidence I have seen,
with unwinding, the idiomatic lock().unwrap() picks the worst option of all.
That’s because it neither stops the process nor lets it continue as it will turn
every further lock into a panic with sometimes disastrous effects.  But that
is not the only issue with the system today.  So here I want to share some of
the issues and with some references to real world code of how people got bitten.
The Error Holds the Lock
One subtle aspect to the poisoning is that the PoisonError needs to hold the guard.
That’s because in order to ignore the poison flag, you need to fetch the guard
from the error object.  Holding on to the error means holding on to the lock!
That can cause common code that does error wrapping / error conversions into a
deadlock hazard.  The innocent looking m.lock()? in a function returning
Box<dyn Error> or similar keeps the mutex locked for as long as the error
lives (#159930).
This can also happen with if let.  For instance in
cc-switch
you can see that they had a test hung because a if let Ok(..) = lock() { .. } else { .. } fallback locked the same mutex again while the unnamed
PoisonError from the condition still owned the guard.
PC-AI had the same bug
in a match arm.  Another case can be found in
ox-embed-server.
Panic To Outage
Deviously poisoning does not fail fast and done wrong, it fails forever.  The
original panic happens once, on one thread, often somewhere unrelated from future
failures.  Every later lock().unwrap() on that lock now however panics as
well, and because so much Rust code survives panics (thread pools, request
handlers, tokio tasks, FFI boundaries), the process stays up and becomes
useless:
In RLS a failed cargo build panicked with ENV_LOCK held which made any
subsequent runs impossible.
Mozilla’s
application-services
saw PoisonError rise to rank
5 in crash
stats and moved to
parking_lot after
they concluded they did not benefit of poisoning handling.
A Neon safekeeper on
staging failed every timeline lookup after a panic with a global lock held,
and the original panic could not even be found in the logs.
While not live services, test suites show the same general issue.  One failing
test poisons a shared static and every test after it fails with PoisonError.
This problem showed up for
cargo,
deno,
polars and
rustc
itself.
Attempt At Recovery
If you recover with into_inner(), the flag stays set and every later access
takes the recovery path again.  And remember that for the first nine years of
Rust after the poisoning feature landed, you could not even clear it as
clear_poison arrived only in 1.77.  Not clearing the flag means that potentially
expensive side effects will happen from that point onwards:
goose-in-a-pond
rebuilt its decoder state on every transcription after a single panic,
librefang
logged the same warning on every access, and a
pool threw its
model away on every return.
Nobody Relies on It, Not Even std
So who is handling poisonings?  I’m really not sure, definitely not the standard library.
Every place where the standard library’s own code ignores it.  Standard I/O has done so since March
2015, two months before
1.0, because “any poison must have been the result of user code which the lock
isn’t protecting”.  A common issue with a lot of poisoning errors that never
had anything to do with the mutex that was held.
Same with the panic output
capture, the backtrace
lock and the WASI
environment lock.  They
all do the same and unsurprisingly there is an open
PR to move std’s internal
mutexes to nonpoison.
And I would argue the ecosystem has largely come to the same conclusion.  Tokio’s own locks don’t poison.
Internally it wraps the std one in an adapter that removes poison.  When it landed Carl Lerche remarked “I rather pretend lock poisoning isn’t a
thing.”  In
one case Eliza Weisman needed
into_inner
to unlink a waiter during drop, or “we’ll leave the list with a potentially
dangling pointer”.  I want to point to this in particular because this is a case where poisoning stood in the way of memory safety which is commonly argued as a reason you want poisoning.
Wasmtime, crossbeam-channel, tracing-subscriber always ignores lock poisoning.
rust-analyzer switched to
parking_lot after
cancellation poisoned its solver like RLS did before.  The parking_lot maintainer
described it
as an anti-feature that hurts usability and reliability to which I strongly
concur.
Why Only Mutex?
Another aspect here is why this is done on Mutex but not on RefCell.  Surely
if the case for poisoning is that some code temporarily breaks an invariant, panics, and
someone else observes the broken state, then this should apply to more cases.
Take the usual example that argues in favor of poisoning and replace Mutex
with RefCell, and you have exactly the same
problem.
Threads are not needed at all and this is not hypothetical either as tokio
catches every task panic.  Paired with a LocalSet the panic comes back as a
JoinError, the next borrow() succeeds and reads a null
pointer
exactly like the mutex example from the issue.
Given how much panic catching goes on in async code, much of which is !Send
for performance reasons, I’m not even convinced that panics get caught more
often in multi-threaded code yet nobody asks for RefCell to poison.
The standard library isn’t consistent with itself either as LazyLock poisons
for good, OnceLock never poisons, Mutex poisons but lets you recover.
Also remember that poisoning only tracks panics and a more common early return
has the same issue.  The ? operator (as well as the try! macro before) that
returns early from the middle of a critical section leaves the same broken
invariant behind an unpoisoned lock.
Note also that the coupling of poisoning of mutexes is
historical
and an explicit Poison<T> type would allow you to opt into this for any
interior mutability wrapper.
What I want
Personally I hope the rust team stabilizes std::sync::nonpoison, have
std::sync::Mutex resolve to it by
default.  If someone wants
poisoning add that separate Poison<T> wrapper then anyone who believes they
need and can handle it, can opt into it for any type including RefCell or
tokio threads.
What I think would be the worst of all outcomes is the counter-proposal is to
keep poisoning but have lock() panic instead of returning a Result.  That
would only fix the held guard lock semantics, and to a smaller degree the
ergonomics, but it makes the slow outage the only option.  That is what every
lock().unwrap() does today, and the issues above should be plenty of evidence
of this being a problematic behavior in light of the existence of catch_unwind.
The post In defense of lock
poisoning is the best argument for
the other side and worth reading but I believe the evidence all points the other
way, and most of what Oxide ships aborts on panic anyway which is also a
reasonable behavior.

articles.title: Show HN: Mason – A lightweight Postgres read-replica, built on columnar storage
articles.summary:
Hi HN! TLDR: we’ve built an open-source drop-in replacement for a postgres read-replica, powered by duckdb’s columnar compute engine. It’s very fast. And it looks like postgres.
So, this started out as: let’s just connect Clickhouse to our postgres dbs and throw our analytics queries at it instead. That will speed everything up.  But we quickly found that 1) Clickhouse comes with quite the learning curve (engine optimisation) to make it fast (we needed something we could easily drop in to any customer’s postgres scenario), and 2) we had underestimated how different clickhouse’s SQL syntax was to postgres.  Don’t get me wrong: we love Clickhouse (it’s ridiculously fast if you know what queries to expect), it just didn’t work for our ad-hoc postgres workloads.
So we went searching for alternatives that were 1) more plug-and-play and 2) looked a lot more like postgres.
We dismissed a bunch based on desk research alone:
- pg_mooncake (seems to have stalled since data bricks bought them)
- pg_duckdb (seems to offer fast queries, or fresh data, but not both - we needed both)
- materialize/risingwave/readyset (like Clickhouse, they require knowing the query shapes upfront - not ideal for ad-hoc workloads)
- firebolt (license makes it challenging to offer to our customers)
- redshift / alloydb / etc (we wanted something cloud-provider agnostic)
And we shortlisted 3:
- pg_clickhouse (Postgres extension that parses SQL in Postgres and pushes the work down to ClickHouse)
- cedarDB  (closed-source, Postgres-compatible analytical database)
- duckdb  (open-source, embedded columnar analytics engine with a Postgres-like SQL dialect)
We needed to know how they would perform on real postgres queries, so we took a backlog of 5,410 (hand-written) queries (chosen because they had been slow to execute against postgres) from 159 real postgres databases.  We then generated synthetic data (dynamically using the schemas from those 159 databases) to fill 159 local databases so we could run the experiment.
We then spun up the 3 short-listed tools locally, and ran each of the 5,410 queries against both postgres and the 3 tools, and compared the results:
- pg_clickhouse (matched postgres 59.4% of the time, refused 39.9% of the queries and was “wrong” 0.8% of the time).
- cedarDB (matched postgres 88.1% of the time, refused 8% of the queries and was “wrong” 3.9% of the time).
- duckdb (matched postgres 84.1% of the time, refused 14.3% of the queries and was “wrong” 1.6% of the time).
Matched meant they returned exactly the same result as postgres.  Refused meant they returned an error message (usually telling you some syntax isn’t recognised). And “wrong” meant they didn’t return the same results as postgres.  I appreciate that arguably postgres may be the one that is wrong in some cases - but for our use case, we considered postgres the golden source of truth.
So, both duckdb and cedardb performed pretty well (correctly handled more than 80% of the postgres queries we threw at it), out-of-the box.  But we really still wanted to try and cover that long-tail.
We chose duckdb as its open-source license would allow us to easily work on the long tail to get the postgres SQL parity we wanted.
So, Mason (linked above), is what we built, powered by duckdb, which now matches postgres on 96% of our 5,410 queries, plus hundreds of other queries that we added, testing it with Metabase, Grafana, Superset, DBeaver and Trevor.io.  For the remaining 4%, it errors with a nice clear message telling you how to rewrite your SQL.
We’d love your feedback on what we’ve built.  Useful?  How can we make it better?

articles.title: Comments and emails
articles.summary:
I'm regularly asked why Bear doesn't have built-in comments, guestbooks, or contact forms. They're all trivial to build (a text box and a send button), and I could add them in an afternoon. But they're not included by design.
The problem with all three is what they let in. A comment box or contact form accepts anything from anyone. Spam bots find them quickly, so whoever runs the blog ends up moderating a queue. And the people who comment don't have to identify themselves as most of these forms ask for a name and email address and check neither.
This week a blogger on Bear received a particularly nasty message via an embedded, third-party contact form on their blog, the sender could type anything into the email boxes and press send. It was signed with a fake name, and used the public email address of another blogger, essentially impersonating someone else to stir up trouble. What arrived was, in effect, a shitty, anonymous note.
Anonymous notes are the worst kind to receive. There's nobody to reply to, nothing to block, and the perpetrator doesn't have a social incentive to behave.
This is why Bear's solution to all three is a link with your email address in it (and if you're worried about scrapers, use a dedicated alias or separate address). Your email provider already does the heavy lifting on spam filtering, and a message generally has to come from a real account you can reply to or block. A contact form would have to recreate that verification with confirmation links, and most don't bother.
Naturally, people can still get nasty emails from throwaway accounts, but the sender still has to set up that account or alias first, which adds just enough friction to discourage it. I suspect most nastiness online is impulsive, and the friction of email is just enough to let that impulse pass.
I wrote recently that good systems are ones that well-behaved people barely notice. Email works the same way. A reader who wants to say they enjoyed your post already has an address, and is happy for you to see it. Someone wanting to stay completely anonymous to send a shitty email has to go out of their way to set it up.
If you'd like readers to be able to reach you, the docs explain how to set up a reply via email link and a guestbook that runs on email.
And if you think I'm wrong about any of this, you can get in touch with me here.

articles.title: Launch HN: Versine (YC F26) – MCP to send and receive money
articles.summary:
Hey HN, we’re Harshith, Param, and Vishnu and we're building Versine (https://versine.com). Versine lets you send and request money just by talking or texting with your AI (think Venmo with an MCP). We’re software engineers who have worked on distributed systems at Stripe, Databricks, and Amazon.
Versine is an MCP that sits in front of a wallet with a balance. With it, your agent can do things like:
- Send money to someone with your approval (via passkey in our app)
- Send and request money to/from up to 100 people at once
- Send money to people without a Versine account (they cash out to their bank in 2 mins)
- Pay people without your explicit approval to trusted contacts (you can set this)
Here’s a demo: https://youtube.com/shorts/Q9X7zioEqi0
We started working on this because assistants are frustratingly hands-off when it comes to finance and money movement. You can have your assistant go through a receipt and map out all the amounts owed taking care of splitting the subtotal, taxes, tips, but at the end of it the assistant hands back work to you when you have to go out and make the Venmo transfer.
Our current solution is oriented towards power users: those who want to automate everything through their agent use us to split dinners, group trips, or settle poker ledgers. We see ourselves unlocking more value for the general consumer as
1. More people turn into power users of agents, and
2. We expand to a more complete banking solution: deposits, transfers, wires, everything you can (and more) do with your bank offered as an MCP.
Behind the scenes, each user has a self-custodial stablecoin wallet storing USDC on Base. With self-custodial wallets, users own their keys, meaning money can’t be sent without their approval.
Interestingly, we were almost forced into this solution because we had around 4 weeks to build this product (after a pivot), and traditional fiat with a partner bank would have caused far too many regulatory and compliance slowdowns.
Because of that, the only fast option that remained was using stablecoin wallets. It also ensures we aren't a Money Services Business (MSB) since we don’t hold control or access to the user’s funds.
Each call to the wallet creates what we call one-time or recurring standing permissions. For a one-time payment, your agent makes an MCP call, and you receive a notification in our mobile app. Once you swipe up in the app and approve with a passkey (or your device’s biometric method), we create a one-time permission that instructs your wallet to send $X to your recipient’s address.
Trusted contacts let your agent send money to people that you’ve previously authorized without explicit passkey approval. Generally, these are people that you’d trust to send your money back even if your agent made a mistake.
We’re also able to support sending money to someone off Versine using claim forwarding, where the user authorizes us to forward a specific amount to a future address (which we create once we verify a recipient's OTP).
Param worked on scaling vector search at Databricks and harness evals at Glean. Harshith worked on core Stripe Connect fee-processing infrastructure and built an AWS Fargate autoscaler at Amazon. Vishnu worked on intent-based agent testing infrastructure at Amazon. None of us were experienced in stablecoin or crypto infra before working on Versine but our distributed systems experience has helped us a lot.
We'd love for you guys to try it! It's available on iOS and Android and as an MCP on ChatGPT and Claude. We also support a public MCP and REST API for other agents.
Please let us know how you find it and if it works as you'd hoped!

The rationale for this rally is that Huang is the central figure
of the AI boom — that Nvidia, which powers the AI economy and

exoskeleton around Huang. With him, AI progress and U.S. tech

investor confidence falters, and the AI bubble pops. On November
9, I wrote that, in the eyes of Silicon Valley and Trump,
Huang was too big to fail. For 11 days — the window between
Huang’s departure and his return — it looked like I was wrong and
the shameless era of lol nothing matters in American politics
and technology was winding down. Nope!
The professed logic of those calling for Huang’s return was
nonsensical. The venture capitalists and shareholders
argued that American dominance in the AI race against China
depended on Huang’s ability to do whatever he pleased. This
impunity included allowing Nvidia leeway to potentially skirt U.S.
export controls and get chips into China, and sleeping with an
alleged Chinese intelligence asset. You might be forgiven for
missing the genius of the argument.
The other side of this coin is that Huang’s personal dishonesty — not just to his family but to the entire Nvidia company (which, I guess, includes his family) — and disregard for U.S. national security policy do not matter. It’s one thing to believe (as I do) that a romantic indiscretion shouldn’t necessarily be cause for firing. It’s another thing entirely to argue that integrity doesn’t matter.
Even just putting aside the fact that Donald Trump is singularly responsible — in an objectively unprecedented way — for Nvidia’s board reinstating Huang, the whole thing is part and parcel with Trumpism itself. Should a single extramarital affair rule someone out from elected office? articles.title: Pluralistic: Free lunches (24 Nov 2026)
articles.summary: Today's links Free lunches: Tech's margin is everyone else's opportunity. Hey look at this: Delights to delectate. Object permanence: Hacker v conman (twice); NESPaul; Record industry v DRM; 21 lb cherpumple; The rich don't "earn" their fortunes; Newscorp offers favorable personal coverage for senate votes; UC Davis x pepper spray; Was the Wisconsin vote hacked?; Definitively modeling distributional outcomes in Disney queuing systems. Upcoming books: Like I said, I'll keep writin' 'em. Colophon: All the rest. Free lunches (permalink) An old joke: "Two economists are walking down the sidewalk and one of them points and says, 'Look, there's a $20 bill, right there on the ground!' The other one is dismissive: 'No, if that was a real $20, someone would have picked it up by now.'" If that joke leaves you scratching your head, then you've been lucky enough to avoid the neoclassical economist's view of the world as a market whose participants, in aggregate, know everything about what people are buying and selling. In that world if there's a "free lunch" – like a $20 bill on the sidewalk – someone will have already taken it. Likewise, if there's a seller who's priced their goods at $10 and a buyer who's willing to pay $30, there will be an "arbitrageur" who will be shuttling those $10 goods to those $30 customers and pocketing the difference. Give it enough time and either the seller will raise their price to $30, or the buyer will realize they should only be offering $10. The market will "clear," with everyone getting everything they need in the most efficient way possible, meaning there's no way to improve anyone's position without making someone else worse off: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pareto_efficiency When markets don't behave like this, neoclassicals hunt for "distortions" that prevent the market from performing this continuous balancing trick. "Distortion" is best understood here as a euphemism for "democratic intervention." If you've ever gotten excited about a commonsense policy solution to a serious economic problem (like public grocery stores as a means of addressing food deserts and greedflation), only to see it shot down by economists who use a lot of jargon to "prove" that it can't possibly work, you've experienced how well "distortion" doomerism keeps us from having nice things. The economist's allergy to distortions is curiously selective. When a company uses its monopoly power to capture its regulators, or bind its workers to silence, or to erect barriers to entry that keep competitors at bay, somehow that doesn't qualify as a "distortion." Same goes for the situation in which a dominant retailer (Walmart) and a dominant manufacturer (Pepsi) come to a secret agreement to force everyone else to raise prices a ton so that Walmart can raise its prices by a (smaller) ton and still be "the cheapest": https://pluralistic.net/2024/08/14/the-price-is-wright/#enforcement-priorities Economists are in love with the idea of the economy as a self-licking ice-cream cone, a beautiful machine that operates all by itself, processing all the information we inject into it by buying and selling and finding the optimal way to produce more of the things we want best at the lowest prices. But like any love-drunk suitor, economists habitually overlook the market's glaring imperfections. In the self-correcting market, a company with high margins sends up a flare that alerts other, hungrier companies to swarm it, competing to offer the cheapest price. Likewise any company with lots of customers: those crowds of customers should conjure up armies of clever planners and inventors who find more efficient ways to produce the same goods and services and lure those customers away. This is the crux of market orthodoxy, the idea that competition lowers margins, goading sellers to offer better goods at better prices. Don't take my word for it, here's Adam Smith: It is not from the benevolence of the butcher, the brewer, or the baker, that we expect our dinner, but from their regard to their own interest. We address ourselves, not to their humanity, but to their self-love, and never talk to them of our own necessities, but of their advantages. If this is true, then the surest sign of a "market distortion" is persistent high margins and persistent high market-share. Any company that dominates its market and charges far more than its costs is a crisp, $20 bill lying right there on the sidewalk for all to see. If no one picks up that $20, then it's a sure bet that there's a "distorter" who is preventing the market from acting on the "information" that there is an opportunity here. America's business lobby loves distortions, so long as they're the kinds of distortions that let the companies safely entrust their $20 bills to the sidewalk without worrying about having them scooped up by a competitor. Take Big Tech: this is an industry with such persistently high margins and so many customers that there are multiple firms in the sector that were able to piss away hundreds of billions of dollars by manipulating their stock prices with buybacks and building AI data-centers that can never turn a profit: https://pluralistic.net/2025/09/06/computer-says-huh/#invisible-handcuffs If the market was "undistorted" then anyone this rich and this stupid would be in serious trouble. Ask a neoclassical to explain Big Tech's prolonged, morbid wealth and they'll insist that this means that we're the stupid ones, because we can't play 11-dimensional chess like Zuckerberg, which is why we can't understand why it was good to piss away $80b on the metaverse. But we don't have to look very hard to find another, simpler explanation. Big Tech owes its profits to its monopoly power, which allows it to form cartels that collude to rig prices: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jedi_Blue Big Tech has so much money that it can capture its regulators, securing favorable laws that make it literally illegal to build competing products, so we're all stuck as hostages of the platforms: https://pluralistic.net/2026/01/14/sole-and-despotic/#world-turned-upside-down An "undistorted" market is one where information is presumed to flow freely among market participants. But the business lobby has secured far-reaching legal protection for the nondisclosure and noncompete "agreements" it crams down the throats of its workers, customers and suppliers, making it literally illegal to warn other people about the defects in both its products and its managers' character: https://pluralistic.net/2026/06/27/zuckerstreisand-2/#autodisparagement An "undistorted" market is one in which the state intervenes to enforce contracts. Without that intervention, cheaters can beat trustworthy competitors by making promises they have no intention of keeping. Yet, the business lobby has secured government backing for "binding arbitration" waivers that make it illegal to sue people who cheat you, forcing you to have your case heard by a fake judge who works for the cheater and nearly always rules in their favor (and whose rulings are legally secret, so you can't warn others so they don't get cheated as well): https://pluralistic.net/2020/04/11/socialized-losses/#justice-restored "Undistorted" markets are supposed to keep firms lean and energetic, forever on the lookout for new ways to attract the best customers and the best workers with the best deals and the best pay. Decades of lax merger enforcement has produced an economy dominated by fat and lazy cartels who substitute bullying and lock-in for innovation and customer service: https://www.openmarketsinstitute.org/learn/monopoly-by-the-numbers The business lobby and their tame economists have invented all kinds of gimmicks to "disprove" your intuition that you're worse off every year thanks to cheaters and their rising profits. For example, there are plenty of mainstream economists who insist that the wage stagnation that has trapped American workers for decades is a hoax. They point to statistics that show that when you include "transfers," American workers are doing just as well as their foreign counterparts, and in particular, that the American public continues to enjoy healthy levels of "consumption" (buying things). These are very dodgy stats indeed. Here's how they're calculated: the American consumption figures include the health care received by the American public. That health care includes Medicare payments on behalf of Americans who age out of employer-provided insurance, and Medicaid payments made on behalf of poor Americans. These medical services cost 200-300% more than the same services when provided in other advanced economies (Canada, Germany, the UK, etc). So when a poor American in Buffalo gets Medicaid dialysis at three times the price of a dialysis session in Toronto, that is counted toward that poor person's consumption levels, as though they had just gone out and spent hundreds of dollars on treats from the Cheesecake Factory and the Apple Store. In reality, they've received an overpriced service (whose costs were absorbed by the public purse). They haven't seen an extra dime to spend on either the necessities of life or a little treat: https://capitalisnt.com/episodes/can-capitalism-be-popular-FcXPThM6 America spends more on health-care than any other rich nation, and gets less for its money than anyone else. In other words: neoclassical economists use the sky-high monopoly prices set by America's overpriced, underdelivering health care cartel to claim that we've got tons of "real" income, because they factor in the hundreds of billions in public subsidy the feds and the states funnel to these persistently high-margin (and therefore definitively inefficient) businesses. Get rid of the statistical mirages and a very different America comes into focus: one in which large businesses have fused with a corrupted state that serves as bagman and enforcer for the corporate sector as it rips off workers and consumers. Remember the decades when tech bros insisted that their "disruption" was all in service to shattering the death grip that legacy industries had on our economy? Uber's early champions insisted that the taxi sector had been "distorted" by overreaching regulation. Once Uber injected "information" about willing riders and willing drivers into the system, the market would clear, pairing drivers and riders in such a way that no one could be made better off without making someone else worse off. Today, Uber uses its lock-in to pay drivers less and less and charge riders more and more – and Uber uses IP law to prevent competitors from making an app that lets drivers automatically shop for better pay and apps that let riders find cheaper rides: https://pluralistic.net/2026/07/11/your-risk/#my-reward Uber's "perfect market" is a government-backed monopoly, reliant on the state to block anyone from reverse-engineering its app or unionizing its workers. That fusion of the corporation and the state funnels billions from drivers and riders to investors. Amazon's founding principle is best summed up in Jeff Bezos's oft-repeated motto, "Your margin is my opportunity." Today, 51-60% of every sale on Amazon's platform is captured by the platform. AWS, Amazon's cloud service, is no longer its most profitable line of business. Today, Amazon's largest source of profit is the $80b it makes every year from charging for search-placement, extracting bribes from sellers to show you items that cost more than the best match for your query: https://pluralistic.net/2026/09/04/cheating-at-fraud/#absentee-rentier That's a lot of margin – and a lot of opportunity. Same goes for Apple: the company's most profitable line of business is the 30% app tax it levies on every payment made using an iPhone or iPad. Apple makes $100b/year charging a 30% commission on payments that cost the company less than 1% to process. That's a lot of margin. Then there's the ad-tech duopoly, Meta/Google. These two companies make so much money in an ad system where they represent both buyers and sellers in marketplaces they operate (where they also buy and sell), that they have hundreds of billions left to blow on AI misadventures: https://pluralistic.net/2026/10/19/spying-v-context/#unattributed In other words, Big Tech's sidewalk is covered in $20 bills, which the US government bans American firms from picking up. But that's America. What about the rest of the world? Well, for 25 years, the US Trade Representative has made it America's business to see to it that every US trading partner enacted laws that protected America's tech companies from competitors. Thus the UK's pavements are littered with 20 pound notes, and the EU's are covered in 20 euro notes: https://pluralistic.net/2026/01/01/39c3/#the-new-coalition The US Trade Rep used both a carrot and a stick to extract these policy concessions from the rest of the world. The carrot was the promise of tariff-free access to the American consumer (the world's richest, shoppingest, most numerous consumer cohort) – the stick was the threat of tariffs. Today, the stick is broken and the carrot is gone. The American consumer's wallet has been drained. American homeowners groan under multiple mortgages. American renters give 50% of their paycheck to Wall Street slumlords. The US healthcare system has emptied their bank accounts and student debt came for the rest. to the company’s value.
This whole preposterous saga would reek to high hell even if Donald Trump didn’t own a share of stock in any public company. It’s a national security farce and a full-throated embrace of “state capitalism” (per the well-known socialist sympathizers on the WSJ Editorial Board). But given that Trump does own stock in Nvidia, the corruption is prima facie. Who could possibly argue that this is not corrupt? The only possible defense is that everyone is corrupt and if everyone is corrupt, it’s OK when it’s your guy doing it.
This, after “corruption” was the top issue on U.S. voters’ minds in this month’s election — an election in which Trump’s Republican Party took a historical drubbing. Huang’s reinstatement was obviously popular with a certain segment of investors and with the AI-mania wing of the tech industry, but this whole abjectly corrupt affair is wildly unpopular with the electorate writ large.

articles.summary:
Bessent comes across as a far more interesting man than I gave him credit for:
But, in the past two years, Bessent has become one of the most
consequential figures in the Trump Administration. A former White
House official called him “the smartest person in the
Administration, by far.” Jason Miller, a longtime Trump adviser,
said, of the Treasury Secretary, “There’s no other person whose
name comes up more often for V.P. in ’28.” Steve Bannon, Trump’s
former chief strategist, went further: “If Scott Bessent wanted
it, I think he could be the Republican nominee in 2028.”
Let’s take that with a grain of salt. A year ago Bannon was spouting off that it was a sure thing Trump was going to run for — and win — a third term in 2028. Bannon’s a fucking nut.
But it’s hard not to see Bessent as the most likable man in a despicable administration:
Even members of the Trump Administration have been subject to
Bessent’s wrath. In the early days of Trump’s second term, when
Musk and the Department of Government Efficiency were taking a
chainsaw to the federal bureaucracy, Musk installed as acting
I.R.S. commissioner a senior official who had publicly accused the
Biden Administration of slow-walking an investigation into Hunter
Biden’s taxes. Bessent confronted Musk about the move in the Oval
Office. The two exchanged “fuck you”s before the argument spilled
out into the hallway, where, according to Maggie Haberman and
Jonathan Swan, in their book “Regime Change,” Bessent taunted Musk
about his unrealized expectations for doge. “Elon, are the savings
two trillion?” Bessent prodded. “One trillion? A hundred billion?”
In response, Musk threw a shoulder into Bessent’s torso.
A few months later, during a dinner for top Administration
officials at Executive Branch, an exclusive Georgetown club
co-founded by Donald Trump, Jr., Bessent objected to the presence
of Bill Pulte, the Federal Housing Finance Agency director, who,
Bessent had heard, was bad-mouthing him to the President. “Why the
fuck are you talking to the President about me? Fuck you,” Bessent
reportedly told Pulte. “I’m gonna punch you in your fucking face.”
(Later, during testimony before the Senate Finance Committee,
Bessent partially disputed this report, saying, “I actually said I
was going to kick his ass.”)
